newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels say will chase out Mobutu unless he resigns.
newsitem.headline: Rebels say will chase out Mobutu unless he resigns.

text.p: Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila said on Monday his forces would chase President Mobutu Sese Seko out of the capital Kinshasa if Mobutu has not handed over power by the time they arrive.

"If Mobutu hands over power before we enter Kinshasa, I will guarantee his safety and that of his biological family. But if he does not, we will have to chase him away in humiliation," Kabila told a news conference at his headquarters in Lubumbashi.
He said that his rebel movement, the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, was ready to enter Kinshasa within two or three days.
They are now less than 60 km (35 miles) from Kinshasa international airport, which lies about 25 km (18 miles) from the city centre in the direction the rebels are approaching, Kabila added.

Kabila met Mobutu on a South African navy ship on Sunday but they disagreed on arrangements for Mobutu to step down. Mobutu wants to hand over power to some transitional body, Kabila wants to take full control immediately.
"I once again appeal to Mobutu to hand over power peacefully to me but if he does not do so my forces are ready to enter Kinshasa in the next two to three days," Kabila said.
In Kinshasa however life went on as normal on Monday despite the rebel advance and the deadlock between Mobutu and Kabila at weekend peace talks on a South African ship.
Witnesses at Ndjili international airport reported that Mobutu's plane had returned. There was no sign of extra checkpoints in the centre of the city of five million people.

Emergency rule Prime Minister Likulia Bolongo met the plane but public access was restricted and although a motorcade with smoked glass windows was seen leaving the airport no one actually saw the veteran president.
Rebels said they would push on towards Kinshasa on several fronts while Mobutu, 66, considered a demand from Kabila for his immediate resignation.

Mobutu offered at Sunday's talks with Kabila and South Africa's Nelson Mandela to hand power to an elected president. Kabila said his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire should serve as transitional authority.
Mandela said fresh talks between Mobutu and Kabila, 56, would take place within eight to 10 days to "narrow the gap between the two parties".
Church sources said the rebels reached their new positions in one day, advancing from their previous forward base at Kenge, 200 km (125 miles) from Kinshasa.

A South African official said Mobutu's offer made on the converted icebreakeer SAS Outeniqua to hand over to an elected president was rejected, but mediators would work in the next few days on a way for him to cede power to a transitional authority.
"The understanding is that Mr Kabila will want to lead that transitional authority," said the official, who would not be named but added that the idea was not to humiliate Mobutu.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said on Monday 91 Rwandan Hutu refugees died in a stampede on a train taking refugees from the jungle for airlifting back home.
UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg said three people were in critical condition and 75 also in hospital after the disaster on the train from Biaro camp to Zaire's third city of Kisangani.
"We have asked (the rebels) for the train evacuation to be stopped immediately while we assess the situation," he added.

The rebels have won control of about three quarters of Zaire in just seven months and are advancing on several fronts. Kabila's rebellion has all but broken Mobutu's three-decade hold over the mineral rich, but corrupt, state.

Some rebel sources said the rebel alliance would delay the final push on Kinshasa until it had a force of 10,000 to 12,000 troops near the capital. At an airport in the southeastern capital of Lubumbashi hundreds of rebels boarded planes on Sunday for the frontlines.
Troops from the United States, the former colonial power Belgium, France and Britain were in Congo, across the river from Kinshasa, to evacuate Western nationals in the event of trouble.
